ch01.anchor: courtesy name Yingliu
ch01.note: A Chinese man of this milieu carried several names: a given name (here 仰山 Yangshan) and a formal zi or courtesy name (应骝 Yingliu) taken at adulthood and used by peers. Chen also changed his surname from Cheng (程) to Chen (陈) when he entered underground work, a common precaution; the book's title and this translation use the revolutionary name throughout.

ch01.anchor: held the metropolitan degree
ch01.note: The jinshi, the highest degree in the imperial civil-service examinations and the gateway to senior office. A salt commissioner (盐政使) oversaw the lucrative state salt monopoly; the grandfather's rank marks the family as one of real standing before its decline.

ch01.anchor: Commentary on the Water Classic
ch01.note: The Shuijing zhu, a celebrated early-sixth-century work by Li Daoyuan expanding a terse older gazetteer of China's rivers into a vast topographical and folkloric survey. Citing it lends the local lake an ancient pedigree.

ch01.anchor: the filial daughter Cao E
ch01.note: A classic tale of filial devotion. The historical Cao E stele (曹娥碑) is real and famous, chiefly for a riddling inscription later added to it; the drowning legend is traditional rather than documented. Cao'e, the girl's name, was in time given to the river and the county town themselves.

ch01.anchor: national salvation through industry
ch01.note: Shiye jiuguo, the early-twentieth-century conviction that China could be saved by building modern commerce and industry rather than by politics. Chen's abandonment of it for revolution is the arc of this chapter; the parallel slogan 'salvation through education' appears below.

ch01.anchor: the May Fourth Movement broke out in 1919
ch01.note: The student-led protests of May 4, 1919, against the Versailles award of German concessions in Shandong to Japan, which swelled into a nationwide movement for cultural renewal and against imperialism and warlordism. It is conventionally taken as the seedbed of Chinese Communism.

ch01.anchor: the notorious February 7 Massacre
ch01.note: The Erqi incident of February 7, 1923: the warlord Wu Peifu, of the Zhili clique that then controlled the Beijing-Hankou line, crushed the railwaymen's strike by force. It became a founding martyrdom of the Chinese labor movement. The casualty figures here are the book's.

ch01.anchor: more than two thousand li of it
ch01.note: The li is a traditional Chinese unit of distance, in the modern period standardized at half a kilometer; two thousand li is roughly a thousand kilometers, about the length of the Beijing-Hankou line.

ch01.anchor: the magazine China Youth
ch01.note: Zhongguo qingnian, launched in 1923 as the organ of the Socialist Youth League and edited by Yun Daiying, among the most influential progressive periodicals of its day among young readers.

ch01.anchor: the Socialist Youth League of China
ch01.note: The Communist Party's youth organization, founded 1922, from which promising members like Chen graduated into full Party membership; the forerunner of today's Communist Youth League.

ch01.anchor: the League Central secretary, Ren Bishi
ch01.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950), then a very young secretary of the Youth League's central committee, later one of the five top leaders of the CCP alongside Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and Zhu De.

ch01.anchor: the death of Lenin
ch01.note: Lenin died on January 21, 1924; memorial issues of the Chinese left press introduced many young readers, Chen among them, to the Soviet model as a template for China's own revolution.

ch01.anchor: a captive of Chu
ch01.note: The closing image of Yun Daiying's prison poem. 'A captive of Chu' (Chu qiu) is a classical byword, from the Zuo zhuan, for a prisoner who keeps his dignity and loyalty in captivity. The book reproduces the poem in Zhou Enlai's own 1953 hand and prints it as shown here; other published texts of the poem read slightly differently in two characters, a variation left as the book gives it.

ch01.anchor: the May Thirtieth Movement
ch01.note: The nationwide anti-imperialist upheaval of 1925, touched off by the events this section narrates: British-officered police in Shanghai's foreign settlement shooting Chinese demonstrators. It marks the high tide of the mid-1920s revolution.

ch01.anchor: the International Settlement
ch01.note: The foreign-run enclave in central Shanghai, outside Chinese jurisdiction, administered by the Shanghai Municipal Council (the 工部局) with its own police force and, for cases involving Chinese, the Mixed Court. That an armed foreign administration policed Chinese streets is the standing grievance behind this whole episode.

ch01.anchor: the council's chief inspector, McEuen
ch01.note: K. J. McEuen, Commissioner of the Shanghai Municipal Police in 1925. His order to fire and the killings that followed on Nanjing Road on May 30 made him a lasting symbol of the settlement's use of force against Chinese; he was later removed amid the outcry.

ch01.anchor: carried the Northern Expedition victoriously into Hubei
ch01.note: The Northern Expedition (1926-1928), the Kuomintang-Communist military campaign out of Guangdong to defeat the northern warlords and reunify China; its early advance into the central provinces frames much of this chapter's action.

ch01.anchor: the April 12 counter-revolutionary coup
ch01.note: On April 12, 1927, Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai, massacring Communists and labor activists with gangster help and ending the first Kuomintang-Communist united front. The 'white terror' (白色恐怖) that follows in the book is the term for the wave of arrests and killings across the country afterward.

ch01.anchor: an armed uprising at Nanchang
ch01.note: The Nanchang Uprising of August 1, 1927, the Communists' first armed revolt against the Kuomintang after the split; its date is now marked as the founding day of the People's Liberation Army. He Long, then a Kuomintang general, was one of its commanders, which is why he was hunted afterward.

ch01.anchor: a reward of 100,000 silver dollars
ch01.note: The silver dollar (dayang) was the standard hard currency of Republican China; a hundred thousand of them was an enormous bounty, a measure of how badly the Kuomintang wanted He Long.

ch01.anchor: societies and secret sects of men like Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng
ch01.note: Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng were the bosses of Shanghai's Green Gang, the criminal fraternity that ran the city's underworld and that Chiang Kai-shek used as muscle in the April 12 purge; secret sects (会道门) were popular quasi-religious brotherhoods.

ch01.anchor: working in the Central Special Branch
ch01.note: The Zhongyang teke, the CCP's clandestine intelligence and security service in Shanghai, set up under Zhou Enlai after the 1927 split to protect the underground, gather intelligence, and punish traitors. It is the world in which the rest of this book unfolds, and Chen Yangshan's life's work.

ch01.anchor: the traitor Gu Shunzhang
ch01.note: Gu Shunzhang, a senior Special Branch operative whose capture and defection in April 1931 exposed much of the CCP underground and led directly to the deaths of many, including Yun Daiying. His name recurs through this book as its great catastrophe.

ch01.anchor: the Municipal Council's four proposals
ch01.note: Four by-laws the Shanghai Municipal Council put before the 1925 ratepayers' meeting, among them a press-registration rule widely read as censorship and a rise in wharfage dues. Chinese residents, who paid the settlement's rates but had no vote in it, fought the proposals as a further tightening of foreign control, which is why they loom so large here.

ch01.anchor: in the foothills of the Kuaiji range
ch01.note: The Kuaiji (Guiji) range, south of Hangzhou Bay, is among the anciently storied mountains of China: the legendary sage-king Yu the Great is said to be buried there, and it was nearby, at the Orchid Pavilion in 353 CE, that the calligrapher Wang Xizhi held his celebrated gathering.

ch01.anchor: came originally from Huizhou prefecture in Anhui
ch01.note: Huizhou, in southern Anhui, was the home of the Huizhou merchants (徽商), one of imperial China's two great merchant networks and a byword for commercial wealth married to Confucian respectability — the standing this declining family had once had.

ch01.anchor: moved during the Xianfeng years to Shaoxing prefecture
ch01.note: Shaoxing, in eastern Zhejiang, is an old water town famous for its rice wine and, in this period, for supplying the empire's offices with legal secretaries (绍兴师爷); it is also the birthplace of the writer Lu Xun. The Xianfeng years (1851–1861) were the reign in which the Taiping wars raged.

ch01.anchor: was a failed licentiate
ch01.note: The xiucai or 'licentiate' was the lowest imperial examination degree, won at the county level; it brought gentry standing and exemption from corporal punishment but no office or income. Chen's father held it and rose no higher, hence 'a poor scholar.'

ch01.anchor: an apprentice at a money shop in Wuhan
ch01.note: Wuhan is the conurbation of three towns where the Han River meets the Yangtze: Wuchang on the south bank (the old administrative city), with Hankou and Hanyang opposite, Hankou being the great commercial port. A 'money shop' (钱庄) was a traditional Chinese private bank.

ch01.anchor: During the Taiping upheaval
ch01.note: The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), a vast religious-political civil war against the Qing led by Hong Xiuquan, who proclaimed a 'Heavenly Kingdom' at Nanjing. Perhaps twenty million died before it was crushed; the family fled its reach into Zhejiang.

ch01.anchor: On February 7 the warlords Cao Kun and Wu Peifu
ch01.note: Cao Kun (1862–1938) headed the Zhili clique of Beiyang warlords and, notoriously, bought the presidency of the Republic in 1923 by bribing the parliament; Wu Peifu was his chief general and the real power on the Beijing-Hankou line.

ch01.anchor: the Communist Lin Xiangqian
ch01.note: Lin Xiangqian (1892–1923), a locomotive worker and union leader at Jiang'an, killed as the passage describes. With Shi Yang he became one of the founding martyrs the February 7 strike gave the labor movement.

ch01.anchor: Shi Yang, legal adviser
ch01.note: Shi Yang (1889–1923), a Wuhan lawyer who defended workers without fee and counseled the railway unions; executed on February 15, 1923. He is remembered as the movement's 'labor lawyer' (劳工律师).

ch01.anchor: joined with the Chinese Kuomintang under Sun Yat-sen
ch01.note: Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925), leader of the 1911 revolution that overthrew the Qing and founder of the Kuomintang, revered by Nationalists and Communists alike as father of the Republic. His 1924 policy of alliance with the Communists and Soviet Russia made the united front of these years possible.

ch01.anchor: built a revolutionary united front
ch01.note: The First United Front (1924–1927): on Sun Yat-sen's initiative and with Soviet advice, Communists joined the Kuomintang as individuals to make a common revolution against the warlords. Its violent collapse in 1927 is the hinge of this whole chapter.

ch01.anchor: chief political instructor at the Whampoa Military Academy
ch01.note: The Whampoa (Huangpu) Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 with Soviet help to officer the united front's army. Chiang Kai-shek was its commandant and Zhou Enlai headed its political department; its graduates went on to lead both the Nationalist and the Communist armies.

ch01.anchor: He was a reader of New Youth
ch01.note: New Youth (新青年), the journal Chen Duxiu founded in 1915 that led the New Culture Movement — championing plain-language writing, science, and democracy, and after 1919 Marxism. It was the intellectual seedbed of the May Fourth generation.

ch01.anchor: Chen Tanqiu took Chen Yangshan aside
ch01.note: Chen Tanqiu (1896–1943), a Hubei teacher who was one of the thirteen delegates to the CCP's First Congress in 1921; executed in Xinjiang in 1943.

ch01.anchor: where Xiang Ying relayed
ch01.note: Xiang Ying (1898–1941), a Wuhan textile worker who rose high in the Party and the labor movement; later political commissar of the New Fourth Army, killed in 1941 after the New Fourth Army (Anhui) Incident.

ch01.anchor: Lin Yunan, secretary of the Wuhan district committee
ch01.note: Lin Yunan (1898–1931), whose full life the book gives below, was a leading labor organizer. He would be among the twenty-four Communists shot together at Longhua in Shanghai on February 7, 1931 — the 'Longhua martyrs,' a disaster traced to Gu Shunzhang's betrayal.

ch01.anchor: an older cousin of Lin Biao
ch01.note: Lin Biao (1907–1971), later one of the Communists' foremost commanders, a marshal, and Mao Zedong's designated successor — until he died in a plane crash in 1971 while, by the official account, fleeing a failed coup. The family gave several sons to the revolution.

ch01.anchor: together with He Mengxiong
ch01.note: He Mengxiong (1898–1931) and Li Qiushi (1903–1931), Communist labor and youth leaders, died with Lin Yunan among the Longhua Twenty-Four; He Mengxiong had just before opposed the Party leadership's ultra-left line.

ch01.anchor: Yang Xingfo spoke first
ch01.note: Yang Xingfo (Yang Quan, 1893–1933), an American-trained scientist and associate of Sun Yat-sen, later secretary of the China League for Civil Rights; assassinated by Kuomintang agents in 1933.

ch01.anchor: the Japanese cotton mills in Qingdao and Shanghai
ch01.note: The Japanese-owned cotton mills, of which the Naigai Wata (内外棉) company ran some of the largest in Shanghai, were centers of the worst industrial conditions and of the labor struggles that led to the May Thirtieth Movement.

ch01.anchor: The Communist Gu Zhenghong, in the front rank
ch01.note: Gu Zhenghong (1905–1925), a Communist worker at a Naigai mill shot dead by a Japanese overseer on May 15, 1925; his killing was the spark that lit the May Thirtieth Movement two weeks later.

ch01.anchor: and Liu Hua, chairing the meeting
ch01.note: Liu Hua (1899–1925), a young Communist and leader of the West Shanghai workers; seized during the movement by the Settlement's police and secretly put to death in December 1925.

ch01.anchor: along the roads of the International Settlement
ch01.note: Nanjing Road, where the shooting below took place, was and is Shanghai's chief commercial street, running through the heart of the International Settlement; the massacre there on May 30, 1925, gave the movement its name.

ch01.anchor: poured toward the Louza patrol house
ch01.note: The Louza (Laozha, 老闸) police station on Nanjing Road, from which the Settlement's British-officered police opened fire on the crowd demanding the arrested students' release.

ch01.anchor: the printing workers of the Zhabei district of Shanghai, led by Chen Yun
ch01.note: Chen Yun (1905–1995), then a young printing worker and union organizer, later one of the most powerful leaders of the People's Republic and the principal architect of its planned economy.

ch01.anchor: made up of Zhou Enlai, Wang Yifei, Nie Rongzhen
ch01.note: Nie Rongzhen (1899–1992), later a marshal of the People's Liberation Army and the director of China's nuclear-weapons program. Yan Changyi (1898–1929), a military organizer, was executed in Shanghai in 1929.

ch01.anchor: Comrades Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Chen Yannian
ch01.note: Mao Zedong (1893–1976), the future leader of the People's Republic, was then a rising Party organizer of the peasant movement. Zhou Enlai (1898–1976), who in these years ran the Party's Shanghai underground and its Special Branch, is the presiding figure of this whole book and Chen Yangshan's ultimate chief.

ch01.anchor: the Fengtian warlord Zhang Zuolin
ch01.note: Zhang Zuolin (1875–1928), the 'Old Marshal,' warlord ruler of Manchuria and head of the Fengtian clique, who then held Beijing. He had the Party's co-founder Li Dazhao hanged in 1927 and was himself killed the next year by a Japanese bomb.

ch01.anchor: Li Dazhao, Zhao Shiyan, Chen Yannian
ch01.note: Leading Communists killed in the 1927 terror. Li Dazhao (1889–1927), co-founder of the Party with Chen Duxiu, was hanged in Beijing by Zhang Zuolin; Chen Yannian (1898–1927) was Chen Duxiu's elder son; Zhao Shiyan, Xiao Chunü, Wang Shouhua, and Xiong Xiong were labor and youth leaders executed in Shanghai and elsewhere.

ch01.anchor: the treachery of Chiang Kai-shek and Wang Jingwei
ch01.note: Chiang Kai-shek (1887–1975), commandant of the Whampoa academy and commander of the Northern Expedition, who broke with the Communists in April 1927, led the Nationalist government thereafter, and after 1949 ruled Taiwan. His fellow-'traitor' here is Wang Jingwei (see below).

ch01.anchor: The general secretary, Chen Duxiu, was removed
ch01.note: Chen Duxiu (1879–1942), founder of New Youth and co-founder and first general secretary of the CCP. Blamed for the catastrophe of 1927 as 'right opportunism' — for subordinating the Party to the Kuomintang — he was removed here and later expelled; the charge is the Party's own framing of a defeat with many authors.

ch01.anchor: of five men: Zhang Tailei, Zhou Enlai, Li Lisan
ch01.note: The provisional leadership after Chen Duxiu's fall. Zhang Tailei (1898–1927) would die weeks later leading the Guangzhou Uprising; Li Lisan gave his name to the reckless 'Li Lisan line' of 1930; Zhang Guotao later rivaled Mao and in 1938 defected to the Nationalists; Li Weihan long served in the leadership.

ch01.anchor: He Long, Zhu De, Ye Ting, Liu Bocheng
ch01.note: The commanders of the Nanchang Uprising, all later giants of the Communist army. He Long and Zhu De (a founder and commander-in-chief of the Red Army) became marshals; Ye Ting led the uprising's troops and later the New Fourth Army; Liu Bocheng, the 'One-Eyed Dragon,' became a marshal and the army's leading strategist.

ch01.anchor: after the Party's August 7 Conference
ch01.note: The emergency conference of August 7, 1927, which met after the united front's collapse, ousted the Chen Duxiu leadership for good, put Qu Qiubai at the head, and set the Party on the course of armed uprising and land revolution. Mao Zedong's saying that 'political power grows out of the barrel of a gun' was uttered here.

ch01.anchor: Qu Qiubai held that He Long
ch01.note: Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), essayist and Party leader who headed the CCP after the August 7 Conference; captured and executed by the Nationalists in 1935, leaving a famous, unsparingly self-doubting last testament.

ch01.anchor: the situation in western Hunan, He Long said
ch01.note: Western Hunan (Xiangxi), the rugged, ethnically mixed border country that was He Long's home ground, where he now proposed to raise a force; it became the nucleus of the Hunan-western-Hubei revolutionary base.

ch01.anchor: settled He Long together with Zhou Yiqun
ch01.note: Zhou Yiqun (1896–1931), He Long's close comrade and co-founder with him of the Honghu base in the Hunan-Hubei lake country; killed in 1931.

ch01.anchor: and He Long, Guo Liang, Xu Teli
ch01.note: Among the nucleus were veterans of standing: Xu Teli (1877–1968), a schoolmaster who had taught the young Mao Zedong and joined the Party at fifty, and Guo Liang (1901–1928), a Hunan labor leader soon executed by the Nationalists.

ch01.anchor: on November 17 with Liu Bocheng and Lin Boqu
ch01.note: Lin Boqu (1886–1960), a founding elder of the Party (one of the 'Five Elders' of Yan'an) and later a senior statesman of the People's Republic.

ch01.anchor: guarded by Lu Dongsheng
ch01.note: Lu Dongsheng (1908–1945), a former oil-mill hand who became He Long's bodyguard and in time a general; he died in an accident in 1945.

ch01.anchor: Luo Qingchang wrote an essay in his memory
ch01.note: Luo Qingchang (1918–2014), a career intelligence officer who worked under Zhou Enlai and eventually headed the Party's Central Investigation Department; his memorial essay lends this account both its insider authority and its partisan warmth.

ch01.anchor: a Kuomintang member (of the left) named Bao Junfu
ch01.note: Bao Junfu (also known as Yang Dengying, 1900–1969), the Kuomintang intelligence man whom Chen Yangshan would later turn into one of the Communists' most valuable double agents inside the enemy's secret service — a story the chapters ahead tell.

ch01.anchor: arrested by a British constable at the Ewo cotton mill
ch01.note: The Ewo (Yihe, 怡和) mill belonged to Jardine, Matheson & Co., the great British trading house of the China coast; the arrest was made by a constable of the foreign Settlement's own police.

ch01.anchor: on the execution ground at Yuhuatai in Nanjing
ch01.note: Yuhuatai ('Terrace of the Rain of Flowers'), a hill just south of Nanjing that the Nationalist government used as an execution ground; great numbers of Communists and others were shot there, and it is now a memorial park.

ch01.anchor: gave his life at Longhua in Shanghai
ch01.note: Longhua, on Shanghai's southern edge, held the garrison headquarters and its killing ground; the twenty-four Communists shot here on February 7, 1931, Lin Yunan among them, are honored as the Longhua Martyrs.

ch01.anchor: director of the general investigation bureau of the Jin-Sui Border Region
ch01.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Border Region was a Communist base on the north China frontier during the war against Japan, where Chen Yangshan ran intelligence under He Long — the wartime posting the book's later chapters reach.

ch01.anchor: escort Comrade He Long smoothly to the Honghu region
ch01.note: Honghu (Hong Lake), the marshy lake country on the Hunan-Hubei border where He Long and Zhou Yiqun built their soviet base after 1928.

ch01.anchor: the revolutionary masses in the days of the great revolution
ch01.note: 'The Great Revolution' (大革命) is the standard Chinese name for the national revolutionary upheaval of 1924–1927 — the united front, the mass movements, and the Northern Expedition — brought down by the 1927 split.

ch01.anchor: a member of the National Revolutionary Military Commission of the Soviet areas
ch01.note: The 'Soviet areas' (苏区) were the rural base areas the Communists governed as local soviets — workers'-and-peasants' councils on the Russian model — after 1927; the Jiangxi Soviet was the largest.

ch02.anchor: The Central Guard Regiment is a name people know today
ch02.note: The unit that guards the Party’s top leaders. The author opens by measuring the secret Special Branch of the 1920s against this familiar modern body; the comparison is his own framing device.

ch02.anchor: the Second Revolutionary Civil War
ch02.note: The Communist name for the period 1927–1937, from the collapse of the first Kuomintang-Communist alliance to the outbreak of full war with Japan; also called the Agrarian Revolutionary War.

ch02.anchor: the Autumn Harvest Uprising that Mao Zedong led in Hunan
ch02.note: A Communist rising of September 1927 on the Hunan-Jiangxi border. Defeated in the towns, Mao Zedong led the remnant up into the Jinggang Mountains, a turn later treated as the birth of the Red Army’s rural strategy.

ch02.anchor: on Jinggangshan in Jiangxi
ch02.note: The Jinggang Mountains, on the Hunan-Jiangxi border, where Mao and Zhu De built the first rural revolutionary base in 1927–28.

ch02.anchor: Su Zhaozheng
ch02.note: A leader of the 1925–26 Hong Kong–Guangzhou strike and one of the Party’s foremost labor organizers; he died of illness in 1929.

ch02.anchor: Luo Yinong
ch02.note: A leader of the Shanghai workers’ uprisings of 1927; arrested and executed by the Kuomintang in Shanghai in April 1928. He is the “Luo Yinong” Zhou Enlai names below.

ch02.anchor: Peng Pai
ch02.note: Organizer of the Hailufeng peasant soviets in Guangdong, among the earliest in China; captured and executed in Shanghai in 1929, one of the four comrades whose rescue is described later in this chapter.

ch02.anchor: Deng Zhongxia
ch02.note: A pioneer labor leader and Party theorist; executed by the Kuomintang in 1933.

ch02.anchor: from the East River front
ch02.note: The Dongjiang (East River) region of eastern Guangdong, where the scattered forces of the Nanchang Uprising had made their last stand.

ch02.anchor: following the special-work office of the Wuhan Military Commission before it
ch02.note: A short-lived intelligence unit under the Party’s military commission in Wuhan in early 1927, generally counted the immediate forerunner of the Central Special Branch.

ch02.anchor: working the revolutionary two-faced policy
ch02.note: The tactic of a covert agent living a double life, outwardly serving the enemy while secretly working for the Party; a fixed term of art in Communist underground work.

ch02.anchor: its chief was Hong Yangsheng
ch02.note: Hong Yangsheng, chief of the Special Branch’s General Affairs (First) Section.

ch02.anchor: planted Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, Hu Di, and others
ch02.note: The three agents the Party planted inside the Kuomintang’s own intelligence apparatus, later famed as the “Three Heroes of Longtan.” Li Kenong became after 1949 the Party’s senior intelligence official.

ch02.anchor: rescued leading cadres such as Ren Bishi and Guan Xiangying
ch02.note: Guan Xiangying, then a Communist Youth League leader, later a senior political commissar; his rescue is told at length later in this chapter.

ch02.anchor: eliminated the traitors He Jiaxing, Bai Xin
ch02.note: He Jiaxing and his wife informed on the Party and were assassinated by the Red Squad in 1928; Bai Xin, who betrayed Peng Pai and others to their deaths in 1929, was shot by the Red Squad in Shanghai that November. “Traitor” renders 叛徒, one who quit the Party and went over to the enemy; it is the author’s word throughout.

ch02.anchor: Chen Yun took overall charge
ch02.note: Chen Yun, then a rising Party organizer, briefly headed the reorganized Special Branch after Gu Shunzhang’s defection; he became after 1949 one of the Party’s most senior leaders and the architect of its economic policy.

ch02.anchor: with Kang Sheng as his deputy
ch02.note: Kang Sheng (Zhao Rong) here enters the security work he would make his career. He rose to run Party intelligence and became a chief instrument of the Yan’an rectification purges and, later, of the persecutions of the Cultural Revolution; the celebratory tone of this biography sits oddly with his historical reputation.

ch02.anchor: Pan Hannian the Second
ch02.note: Pan Hannian, a leading Communist intelligence operative of the 1930s and 1940s; imprisoned in 1955 on a false treason charge and cleared only posthumously.

ch02.anchor: passed in turn to Wu Hejing and others
ch02.note: The book prints the name as Wu Hejing (武和景); the man is almost certainly Wu Hujing (武胡景), who directed the Special Branch’s residual work after the Party center left Shanghai. Rendered here as printed (see the glossary).

ch02.anchor: also called the "Red Squad,"
ch02.note: The Special Branch’s armed unit (the Third Section), which protected the Party’s organs and carried out the killing of traitors and enemy agents; the underground also called it the “dog-beating squad.”

ch02.anchor: its chief was Li Qiang
ch02.note: Li Qiang built the Party’s first clandestine radio network; after 1949 he served as minister of foreign trade and became an academician for his work in radio engineering.

ch02.anchor: Li Yimang, who worked at the central organs
ch02.note: Li Yimang, later a writer and diplomat. The book’s parenthetical “also known as Li Kuntai” is an error: Li Kuntai was the birth name of Li Yichao, that is, Zhao Yiman, the young woman playing his sister in the next line, not of Li Yimang himself.

ch02.anchor: saw the film Zhao Yiman
ch02.note: Zhao Yiman (born Li Kuntai, alias Li Yichao) was a Communist resistance heroine, captured and executed by the Japanese in the Northeast in 1936. The 1950 film Zhao Yiman made her a household name, which is how, the story goes, Li Yimang recognized his onetime “sister.”

ch02.anchor: kept by the married couple Xiong Jinding and Zhu Duansui
ch02.note: Xiong Jinding, the accountant who ran the Party’s covert Shanghai finances under the cover of the Fuxing cloth firm, and Zhu Duansui, the young woman comrade sent to be his “wife”; as the passage recounts, the sham marriage became a real one.

ch02.anchor: a Sichuan restaurant on Fourth Avenue
ch02.note: Fourth Avenue (四马路), today Fuzhou Road, a street of restaurants, bookshops, and teahouses in the International Settlement.

ch02.anchor: Zhou Enlai, Li Weihan, Deng Xiaoping, and the others
ch02.note: Deng Xiaoping, then in his early twenties and working in the Party’s Shanghai central apparatus; later the paramount leader of China from the late 1970s. His recollection of being shielded by the Special Branch appears at the close of this section.

ch02.anchor: Central Circular No. 25
ch02.note: A directive of the Party center, dated December 31, 1927, authorizing the planting of agents inside enemy organs; quoted here from its text.

ch02.anchor: built working ties inside the concession police
ch02.note: The police of the foreign concessions—the Shanghai Municipal Police in the International Settlement, the French concession police in the French quarter—were beyond Kuomintang control, and the Special Branch worked assiduously to place informants and cultivate officers within them.

ch02.anchor: the Songhu Garrison Command
ch02.note: The Kuomintang military garrison for the Shanghai-Wusong area, which held wide powers of arrest and execution over the Chinese-administered city.

ch02.anchor: the yellow unions
ch02.note: Company or Kuomintang-controlled unions set up to draw workers away from the Communist-led ones; “yellow” is the standard labor-movement term for such bodies.

ch02.anchor: Chen Pengnian, who died on the Long March
ch02.note: A returned Chinese laborer from France who studied in Moscow and infiltrated the French concession police for the Party; not to be confused with the traitor Chen Weinian named later. He is said to have died on the Long March.

ch02.anchor: the Communist University of the Toilers of the East in Moscow
ch02.note: The Soviet academy (KUTV) that trained Asian Communists through the 1920s; many early Chinese Party figures passed through it.

ch02.anchor: the "Three Heroes of Longtan."
ch02.note: Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, and Hu Di, planted at the heart of the Kuomintang secret service. In April 1931 Qian Zhuangfei, working beside its chief Xu Enzeng, intercepted the telegrams announcing Gu Shunzhang’s defection and got word to the Party center in time to save it—the feat that made the three legendary. “Longtan” (dragon’s pool) stands for a place of deadly danger.

ch02.anchor: under the guidance of Li Lisan's "left" line
ch02.note: The ultra-left line associated with Li Lisan, dominant in the Party in 1930, which ordered premature armed uprisings in the cities; it was repudiated within months as reckless adventurism. The scare quotes on “left” are the author’s, marking it as a deviation.

ch02.anchor: Liu Ding, Ouyang Xin, and Chen Yangshan
ch02.note: Liu Ding, later a founder of the Communist ordnance industry, worked in the Special Branch’s Intelligence Section; he reappears below as the “expert” sent to sift the seized documents.

ch02.anchor: sent it to Liu Bocheng, chief of staff
ch02.note: Liu Bocheng, a celebrated Red Army and later PLA commander, made one of the ten marshals in 1955; he was then chief of staff of the Party’s Central Military Commission.

ch02.anchor: the "South China News Agency" in Shanghai
ch02.note: An open news agency the Special Branch ran from March 1931 as cover for intelligence work, using a journalist’s freedom of movement and inquiry.

ch02.anchor: Chen Shouchang
ch02.note: Chen Shouchang (1906–1935), an Intelligence Section worker; later a leader in the Central Soviet, killed in action in 1935.

ch02.anchor: the Nationalists' central police station
ch02.note: So the book has it (国民党中央巡捕房). The reference is to the Central Police Station on Fuzhou Road; the concession police were not in fact Nationalist-run, and the phrasing is the author’s loose usage.

ch02.anchor: up Route Pichon into the deep shade of its plane trees
ch02.note: Route Pichon, a quiet residential street of the French Concession, today Fenyang Road.

ch02.anchor: also called Yang Dengying and Liu Junshan
ch02.note: Bao Junfu went by several names; Yang Dengying (杨登瀛) was the cover name he used inside the Kuomintang secret service, and the name under which Chiang Kai-shek’s order below appoints him.

ch02.anchor: left Meiji Gakuin before completing his course
ch02.note: A Christian college in Tokyo. Bao’s Japanese schooling and fluent Japanese shaped the cosmopolitan, “Western” manner the book keeps remarking on.

ch02.anchor: the YMCA that the Japanese ran in Shanghai
ch02.note: The Young Men’s Christian Association, whose Shanghai branches were a hub of foreign contact and social work.

ch02.anchor: came to know Yang Jianhong
ch02.note: Yang Jianhong, a Green Gang figure who ran the Investigation Section’s Shanghai work until his death in 1928; it was he who first drew Bao Junfu into the secret service.

ch02.anchor: the Green Gang
ch02.note: The largest of Shanghai’s secret-society brotherhoods, deep in the city’s labor, opium, and protection rackets and closely allied with the Kuomintang after the 1927 purge of Communists.

ch02.anchor: a trusted man of Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu
ch02.note: The brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, nephews of Chiang Kai-shek’s mentor Chen Qimei, built and ran the Kuomintang party machine and its civilian secret service, the “CC Clique.” Chen Lifu is a principal figure in this section.

ch02.anchor: the Investigation Section of the Kuomintang Central Organization Department
ch02.note: Set up in 1928, the party’s first secret service and the forerunner of the Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong); Bao Junfu became its Shanghai commissioner and, through him, the Communist Special Branch came to staff much of it.

ch02.anchor: the forerunner of the Central Statistics Bureau
ch02.note: Zhongtong, the Kuomintang party’s civilian intelligence and secret-police organ, distinct from the military Juntong (Dai Li’s service).

ch02.anchor: Its first chief was Chen Lifu
ch02.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001), with his brother Chen Guofu the boss of the Kuomintang party apparatus; here at the founding of its secret service. He lived out a long old age in exile in the United States and Taiwan.

ch02.anchor: its second was Zhang Daofan
ch02.note: Zhang Daofan (1897–1968), Paris-trained painter turned Kuomintang cultural official, later head of its propaganda and, in Taiwan, president of the Legislative Yuan. The book paints him as a vain hypocrite; his patronage would later get Bao Junfu out of prison.

ch02.anchor: the "Awakened Lion clique,"
ch02.note: A roll of rival political groupings of the day: the Awakened Lion clique (the Chinese Youth Party, nationalist and anti-Communist), the Anfu clique (a Beiyang-era warlord faction), the Communications clique (financiers around the Bank of Communications), the Reorganizationists (Wang Jingwei’s Kuomintang left), and the Communist Youth League. Chen Lifu’s point is that the new secret service was to watch them all.

ch02.anchor: the Zhabei district committee he belonged to
ch02.note: Zhabei, a working-class district of Chinese-administered Shanghai north of the Settlement; a Communist stronghold.

ch02.anchor: How does Wang Yong sound?
ch02.note: Wang Yong (王庸) became Chen Geng’s cover name in the Central Special Branch, used throughout his Shanghai underground years.

ch02.anchor: Comrades Luo Mai, that is, Li Weihan, and Luo Yinong
ch02.note: Luo Mai was Li Weihan’s Party alias; Luo Yinong, the Shanghai labor leader named earlier, was arrested and shot within months of this, in April 1928.

ch02.anchor: attended the Cairo Conference in Chiang Kai-shek's train
ch02.note: The 1943 summit of Chiang Kai-shek, Roosevelt, and Churchill on the war against Japan.

ch02.anchor: even assigned him a bodyguard, one Lian Desheng
ch02.note: Lian Desheng, a former tram conductor and Communist, served in fact as the Party’s link man to Bao Junfu.

ch02.anchor: An E, of the Central Special Branch
ch02.note: An E, a Communist and later a noted lyricist and writer; she wrote the words of the song “The Fisherman’s Song.” She had been the wife of the playwright Tian Han.

ch02.anchor: formerly Tian Han's wife
ch02.note: Tian Han, dramatist and lyricist, who wrote the words of “The March of the Volunteers,” later the national anthem; he died in prison during the Cultural Revolution.

ch02.anchor: the front page of the China News
ch02.note: The Zhongguo xinwen bao, a Shanghai daily; the “handwritten order” quoted is Chiang Kai-shek’s personal directive appointing Bao under his alias Yang Dengying.

ch02.anchor: Xu Enzeng, head of the Investigation Section
ch02.note: Xu Enzeng (1898–1985), U.S.-trained electrical engineer who ran the Kuomintang’s civilian secret service (Zhongtong) for some fourteen years. Unknown to him, his trusted deputy’s office was riddled with Communist agents—the “Three Heroes of Longtan” among them.

ch02.anchor: Mao Gong, Tan Shaoliang, Qian Dajun, and Xiong Shihui
ch02.note: Kuomintang men of standing in Shanghai. Mao Gong is the same officer the book calls Mao Naigong (deputy adjutant-general of the Garrison Command) later in this section—the two forms name one man. Qian Dajun and Xiong Shihui were senior Kuomintang generals, both later provincial governors.

ch02.anchor: the Municipal Council
ch02.note: The Shanghai Municipal Council, the governing body of the International Settlement, whose police were the Shanghai Municipal Police. It is the same 工部局 rendered “Municipal Council” in Chapter 1.

ch02.anchor: Lampson, then head of the political branch of the British concession police
ch02.note: The (British) chief of the Shanghai Municipal Police political branch, the Settlement’s anti-Communist section. The book gives the name only as 兰普逊; “Lampson” is a reconstruction of the likely Western original and is not certain.

ch02.anchor: and his deputy Tan Shaoliang
ch02.note: Tan Shaoliang, a Chinese detective officer of the Settlement police who worked closely with Bao Junfu.

ch02.anchor: Ye Xiufeng, and Xu Enzeng
ch02.note: Ye Xiufeng, a senior figure of the Kuomintang’s CC-Clique secret service.

ch02.anchor: Chen Xizeng, chief of the Shanghai municipal police
ch02.note: Head of the Kuomintang’s own police in the Chinese-administered city (as distinct from the concession forces).

ch02.anchor: Peng Pai, Yang Yin, and two other comrades, four in all
ch02.note: Peng Pai and Yang Yin, both members of the Party’s Political Bureau, were seized in Shanghai and, with two others (Yan Changyi and Xing Shizhen), shot at Longhua in August 1929. The rescue attempt failed; the four became celebrated martyrs.

ch02.anchor: the traitors Bai Xin, Dai Bingshi, Chen Weinian, and Huang Dihong
ch02.note: Defectors whose movements the Special Branch tracked in order to neutralize them. Huang Dihong tried in 1930 to betray Zhou Enlai himself and was killed before he could; Chen Weinian is a different man from the loyal agent Chen Pengnian named earlier.

ch02.anchor: Jingye Lane on Ward Road
ch02.note: Ward Road (华德路), today Changyang Road, in the eastern part of the International Settlement; the site of the meeting at which Ren Bishi was seized.

ch02.anchor: Huang Molan received Pan Hannian's instruction
ch02.note: Huang Molan (1907–2017), a Communist working in the Party’s Shanghai apparatus and a noted underground operative; she lived past the age of a hundred and ten.

ch02.anchor: the noted Shanghai lawyer Chen Zhigao
ch02.note: A prominent Shanghai barrister sympathetic to the Communists, later drawn in through Huang Molan’s connections.

ch02.anchor: Chen's father Chen Qishou, a member of the Tongmenghui
ch02.note: The Tongmenghui was Sun Yat-sen’s pre-1912 Revolutionary Alliance; membership marked Chen Qishou as a founding revolutionary of the Republic, a standing that carried weight in the courts.

ch02.anchor: the January 28 Incident of 1932
ch02.note: The undeclared war of January–March 1932, when Japanese forces attacked the Zhabei district of Shanghai and the Chinese 19th Route Army fought back; the fighting reshuffled Nanjing politics and, as the book notes, gave Zhang Daofan his opening to free Bao Junfu.

ch02.anchor: the Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries
ch02.note: A nationwide purge of 1950–51 aimed at former Kuomintang officials, agents, and secret-society and “bandit” figures; it required such people to register and brought many arrests and executions.

ch02.anchor: a major-general chief of staff of the Northwest Field Headquarters
ch02.note: A senior Kuomintang staff officer of the northwestern military command; named here only to show the rank of those who came forward to register.

ch02.anchor: warden of Kuomintang government reformatories and repentance houses
ch02.note: The “repentance house” (反省院) was a Kuomintang institution for the political re-education of captured Communists and leftists, part prison, part indoctrination center; a “reformatory” (感化院) served a like purpose.

ch02.anchor: brought in by Chen Yangshan to plant myself inside the enemy
ch02.note: Bao Junfu’s own 1951 deposition, quoted here, dates his tie to the Party to 1926 and says Chen introduced him into the Party—claims that go further than the narrative above, which has the relationship begin in 1928 and treats Bao throughout as a non-Party agent. The book reproduces his self-serving statement as evidence in his case, not as its own account.

ch02.anchor: the Capital Special Criminal Court in Yangpi Lane
ch02.note: The Kuomintang’s special court for political cases in Nanjing, the capital; Yangpi Lane and Zhanyuan Road were sites of its lockups.

ch02.anchor: Ju Hua, the first president of the municipal court
ch02.note: Ju Hua, first president of the Nanjing Municipal People’s Court under the new government; the book’s narrative in one place misprints the name as Ge Hua, but the letter below and the court’s own address make it Ju.

ch02.anchor: sentencing him to one year's control
ch02.note: “Control” (管制) was a penalty short of imprisonment: the offender lived at home but under police supervision, with his movements and civil rights restricted for a set term.

ch02.anchor: the Peking Union Medical College Hospital
ch02.note: Beijing’s foremost modern hospital, founded by the Rockefeller Foundation; a mark of the care the state now extended to the aged Bao.

ch02.anchor: the suppression of the Merchant Corps revolt
ch02.note: The crushing, in October 1924, of an armed rising by the merchant militia of Guangzhou against Sun Yat-sen’s revolutionary government.

ch02.anchor: the Eastern Expedition against Chen Jiongming
ch02.note: The 1925 campaigns from Guangzhou against the warlord Chen Jiongming, once Sun Yat-sen’s ally turned rival, in which the Whampoa cadets, Chen Geng among them, first proved themselves.

ch02.anchor: the Third Army Group of the Chinese People's Volunteers
ch02.note: The Chinese People’s Volunteers were the forces China sent to fight in the Korean War (1950–53); Chen Geng served among their commanders.

ch02.anchor: In 1955 he was given the rank of general
ch02.note: In the rank system introduced that year, 大将 (rendered here “general”) was the second-highest grade, just below marshal; Chen Geng was one of the ten men who held it.

ch02.anchor: Yang Dezhi, former chief of the general staff
ch02.note: Yang Dezhi (1911–1994), a PLA commander who led Chinese forces in Korea and later served as chief of the general staff.

ch02.anchor: It was Chen Geng's wife, Wang Genying
ch02.note: Wang Genying, a Shanghai labor organizer and Chen Geng’s wife; captured in 1933 through Gu Shunzhang’s betrayal, she was later freed and died at the front in 1939, killed by Japanese troops while with the Eighth Route Army.

ch02.anchor: under cover as a reporter for the Shen Bao
ch02.note: The Shen Bao was Shanghai’s oldest and largest Chinese newspaper; a press card gave an underground worker a plausible reason to move about and ask questions.

ch02.anchor: studying at the Shanghai Fine Arts Academy
ch02.note: The Shanghai Art School, China’s pioneering modern art academy, then a byword for bohemian student life.

ch02.anchor: behind the Wing On Company on Nanjing Road
ch02.note: The Wing On Company was one of the great department stores of Nanjing Road, Shanghai’s main commercial street; the old racecourse stood nearby.

ch02.anchor: Hu Egong, who had been a member of parliament
ch02.note: Hu Egong, a parliamentarian of the early Republic turned secret Communist sympathizer; his standing in the old political world gave him cover and useful connections. The “parliament” is that of the Beiyang (warlord) governments in Beijing.

ch02.anchor: assigned Yang Xianzhen as his assistant
ch02.note: Yang Xianzhen (1896–1992), later a well-known Marxist philosopher, persecuted in the 1960s for his thesis that “two combine into one.”

ch02.anchor: the Party organizations of Tianjin, Beiping, and the Shun-Zhi provincial committee
ch02.note: Beiping was the name Beijing bore from 1928 to 1949, after the Nationalists moved the capital to Nanjing. The Shun-Zhi committee was the Party body for the Hebei region around the two cities; “Shun-Zhi” is the old provincial name Zhili.

ch02.anchor: among them An Ziwen, Zhou Zhongying, Chen Yuandao, and Liu Yaxiong
ch02.note: Responsible cadres of the northern Party. An Ziwen later headed the Party’s Organization Department; Chen Yuandao was executed by the Kuomintang in 1933; Liu Yaxiong, Liu Shaobai’s daughter, was Chen Yuandao’s wife.

ch02.anchor: Just then Liu Shaobai, a member of parliament
ch02.note: Liu Shaobai, a Shanxi parliamentarian and landowner who secretly aided the Party; father of Liu Yaxiong and father-in-law of Chen Yuandao.

ch02.anchor: the Butterfield and Swire wharf in Shanghai
ch02.note: The Taigu (Butterfield & Swire) wharf, run by the British shipping and trading firm that dominated the China coast trade.

ch02.anchor: accompanied by Shao Fumin, a "Red Squad" man
ch02.note: Shao Fumin, a Special Branch operative trained as a dentist and known as a crack shot; a member of the Red Squad, the Branch’s armed unit.

ch02.anchor: in the Ta Kung Pao read a piece of news
ch02.note: The Ta Kung Pao, a leading independent Chinese daily then published in Tianjin.

ch02.anchor: Yin Jian, secretary of the Shun-Zhi provincial committee
ch02.note: So the book prints the name; not further identified here beyond the post.

ch02.anchor: the Northwest Army generals Zhang Kexia and He Jifeng
ch02.note: Two generals of Feng Yuxiang’s Northwest Army who were secret Communists or Communist allies; together they led the Jia-Wang defection to the Communists in 1948, a famous turning of the civil war.

ch02.anchor: Zhang Keyun, alias Zhang Kaiyun, a notorious great traitor
ch02.note: A Tianjin Communist who studied in the Soviet Union, defected on his return, and did grave harm to the northern Party. “Met the punishment he deserved” is the book’s way of recording that the Party had him killed. He is a different man from the loyal general Zhang Kexia named just above.

ch02.anchor: a "dog-beating squad" to Tianjin to suppress them
ch02.note: The underground’s nickname for the Red Squad, the Special Branch’s assassination unit; “beating the dogs” meant killing traitors and enemy agents.

ch02.anchor: the Red Army in the Hubei-Henan-Anhui soviet area
ch02.note: One of the largest Communist base areas of the early 1930s, in the border hills where the three provinces meet; Chen Geng commanded a division there after leaving Shanghai.

ch02.anchor: its open journals Red Flag and Bolshevik
ch02.note: Hongqi (Red Flag) and Buershiweike (Bolshevik) were the Party’s open and semi-open periodicals of the period.

ch02.anchor: a hundred silver dollars
ch02.note: The silver dollar (大洋), the standard hard currency of Republican China; a single dollar was a day’s good wage or more. That Bao’s gift topped a Kuomintang agent’s whole monthly pay of ninety-five is the author’s point.

ch02.anchor: the old stronghold of Nanjing
ch02.note: Nanjing, the Kuomintang capital, here by its old epithet “the coiling dragon and crouching tiger” (虎踞龙盘), a classical phrase for a naturally fortified seat of power; the fall of the city in April 1949 sealed the Communist victory.

ch02.anchor: the National Congress of Soviets on Hart Road
ch02.note: The gathering of delegates from the Communist soviet areas, held in secret in the Shanghai International Settlement in May 1930 to prepare a national soviet government; the source notes it was downgraded from a congress to a conference. The First National Congress of the Chinese Soviet Republic proper met the following year, in November 1931, at Ruijin in Jiangxi.

ch02.anchor: Tan Yubao, just back from study in the Soviet Union
ch02.note: Tan Yubao (1899–1980), named here as the first head of the Red Terror Squad. He later led the three-year guerrilla struggle in the Hunan–Jiangxi border region after the main Red Army set out on the Long March, and held provincial posts in Jiangxi after 1949.

ch02.anchor: another "ruse of self-injury,"
ch02.note: One of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: a man injures himself, or sacrifices his own side, to make the enemy believe a feigned surrender is genuine. Here Dai Bingshi lets his own sister-in-law be arrested to allay Communist suspicion.

ch02.anchor: slaughtered tens of millions of Communists and revolutionary masses
ch02.note: The figure is the author's rhetorical exaggeration. The Party's total membership in 1927 was under 60,000, and estimates of those killed in the Kuomintang white terror of 1927–28 run to the hundreds of thousands (a figure of about 300,000 is often cited), not tens of millions.

ch02.anchor: written with a different character, though it reads the same
ch02.note: Chen Yangshan writes the surname with the character 贺 where the standard accounts write 何; both are romanized He. The traitor is He Jiaxing, secretary to Luo Yinong.

ch02.anchor: On the night of August 24, 1928, five important CCP leaders
ch02.note: The book dates the arrest to 1928, but it fell on 24 August 1929. Bai Xin, the Central Military Commission's own secretary, gave away a meeting at his home in the Huxi district, and Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, Xing Shizhen, and Zhang Jichun were seized; Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, and Xing Shizhen were executed at Longhua on 30 August 1929. The book's own later citation of a newspaper item dated 14 September 1929 confirms the year should be 1929. Standard Party-history accounts corroborate the 1929 dates.

ch02.anchor: the Hai-Lu-Feng revolutionary base in Guangdong
ch02.note: The Hailufeng Soviet, set up by Peng Pai in November 1927 in Haifeng and Lufeng counties of eastern Guangdong: among the first worker-and-peasant soviet governments in China. Nationalist forces crushed it in 1928.

ch02.anchor: reached Fan Zhengbo, a standing committee member of the Kuomintang municipal Party
ch02.note: Fan Zhengbo, a Kuomintang Shanghai municipal Party figure and secret-service man, sheltered the traitor Bai Xin. The Red Squad killed Bai Xin outside Fan's residence, and Fan himself was badly wounded in the attack.

ch02.anchor: Ke Lin and He Cheng had opened the "Dasheng Hospital"
ch02.note: Both were Communist doctors who ran clinics as cover for the Party's Shanghai apparatus. Ke Lin (1900–1991), under the name Ke Dawen, later practiced for years in Macao and became a senior medical administrator in the People's Republic; He Cheng (1901–1992), under the name He Yusheng, was a founder of the army's medical service and later a deputy health minister.

ch02.anchor: the Shanghai Kuomintang organ paper Republican Daily
ch02.note: Minguo Ribao, the Kuomintang's newspaper; its Shanghai edition ran from 1916. The item quoted here, a false story that Bai Xin had been bailed out and sent to Nanjing, was planted to hide that he was the informer and still in the city.

ch02.anchor: at No. 43, Fourth Lane, Hehefang, on Route Joffre
ch02.note: Route Joffre (Xiafei Lu) was a principal avenue of the Shanghai French Concession, today Huaihai Middle Road; Hehefang was a lane off it. Here the Red Squad shot Bai Xin dead on the night of 11 November 1929, an operation corroborated in standard accounts of the Central Special Branch.

ch02.anchor: the post office beside the Sincere Company
ch02.note: The Sincere Company (Xianshi), opened on Nanjing Road in 1917, was one of the first great modern department stores of Shanghai.

ch02.anchor: toward the City God Temple
ch02.note: The City God Temple (Chenghuang Miao) in the old walled city of Shanghai, whose surrounding lanes formed a crowded bazaar district.

ch02.anchor: Wang Shiying, then head of the Central Special Branch
ch02.note: Wang Shiying (1905–1968), a veteran Communist intelligence officer who directed the Central Special Branch in its final phase; later a general and provincial official in the People's Republic.

ch02.anchor: secretary to the Kuomintang agent chief Kang Ze
ch02.note: Kang Ze (1904–1967), a leader of the Blue Shirts and head of the Kuomintang's Special-Operations Corps (biedongdui); a prominent Nationalist intelligence and political-training figure, captured by Communist forces in 1948.

ch02.anchor: Liu Xiang, the warlord of eastern Sichuan
ch02.note: Liu Xiang (1888–1938), the dominant Sichuan militarist of the 1930s, based at Chongqing; he maneuvered to preserve his provincial power against Chiang Kai-shek's encroaching central forces.

ch02.anchor: run by the Sichuan power-holder Liu Hangchen
ch02.note: Liu Hangchen (1896–1975), the leading financier of Liu Xiang's regime, head of the Sichuan provincial finance department and the Sichuan Provincial Bank.

ch02.anchor: sent Chen Chang and his wife Liu Qizhen to Chongqing
ch02.note: The book's own footnote to this name reads: Chen Chang, also called Jia Shaoyi, a native of Yilong county, Sichuan; he joined the Chinese Communist Party in December 1927 and did underground work in Wuhan, southern Henan, and Fujian. During the war against Japan he worked to turn Kuomintang troops at Changsha, Guilin, Shangrao, and southern Anhui, and during the civil war did peasant work at Chongqing, where the Kuomintang arrested him late in 1948. After 1949 he served in the Chongqing public security bureau; persecuted in the 'Left' errors, he was tormented to death in 1960.

ch02.anchor: the organization decided to send Chen Kehan back to Chongqing with him
ch02.note: Chen Kehan (1917–1980), a Communist journalist; later a senior figure at the Xinhua News Agency and a deputy minister of culture in the People's Republic.

ch02.anchor: the Center had sent Feng Xuefeng to Shanghai
ch02.note: Feng Xuefeng (1903–1976), a writer and literary theorist and a veteran of the Long March, sent to Shanghai in 1936 to rebuild the Party's contacts there and to liaise with the left-wing literary world and with Lu Xun.

ch02.anchor: the Juntong Renaissance Society and the Zhongtong CC Clique
ch02.note: Two rival Nationalist secret services. The Renaissance Society (the Blue Shirts) was tied to the military-intelligence apparatus that became Juntong; the CC Clique of the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu ran the party-intelligence apparatus that became Zhongtong. Their rivalry was bitter, and the Communists exploited it.

ch02.anchor: the Red Army had ended the Long March and reached northern Shaanxi
ch02.note: The Long March (1934–35), the Communist forces' fighting retreat of some ten thousand li from the southern soviet areas to a new base in northern Shaanxi, after Nationalist encirclement campaigns broke the Jiangxi Soviet.

ch02.anchor: the anti-Japanese struggle of the people of Suiyuan
ch02.note: Suiyuan, a former province in what is now Inner Mongolia. The Suiyuan campaign of late 1936, in which Chinese forces repelled Japanese-backed Mongol troops, became a rallying cause for the national-salvation movement.

ch02.anchor: the news broadcasts of the Kuomintang's Central News Agency
ch02.note: The Central News Agency (Zhongyang She), the Kuomintang's official wire service, founded in 1924; the Three Chens passed its dispatches off as their own agency's exclusives.

ch03.anchor: The Xi'an Incident, which broke out on December 12, 1936
ch03.note: The Xi'an Incident: on 12 December 1936 the generals Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an to force him to halt the civil war against the Communists and lead a united resistance to Japan. After tense negotiations, in which the Communist Party, through Zhou Enlai, pressed for a peaceful settlement, Chiang was released on 25 December, and the affair is generally credited with bringing about the Second United Front. Corroborated by standard histories; the hidden-front work around it is the book's subject here.

ch03.anchor: to resist the foreign foe we must first pacify within
ch03.note: Chiang Kai-shek's slogan rangwai bi xian annei, usually rendered 'internal pacification before resistance to foreign aggression': the doctrine that the Communists had to be destroyed before Japan could be fought. It was the very policy the Xi'an Incident set out to overturn.

ch03.anchor: Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng, who commanded
ch03.note: Zhang Xueliang (1901-2001), the 'Young Marshal,' warlord of Manchuria and commander of the Northeastern Army, driven from his homeland by the Japanese in 1931; his men, set to fight the Red Army in Shaanxi, increasingly resented the task. After the Xi'an Incident Chiang held Zhang under house arrest for more than fifty years, in China and then Taiwan, until his last years in Hawaii. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: the Seventeenth Route Army, were moved
ch03.note: Yang Hucheng (1893-1949), commander of the Seventeenth Route Army and Chiang's co-captor at Xi'an. Unlike Zhang, he was cashiered and sent abroad, then imprisoned on his return; he and members of his family were murdered by Kuomintang agents at Chongqing in September 1949, on the eve of the Communist victory. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: at the Huaqing Pool at Lintong
ch03.note: The Huaqing Pool at Lintong, a hot-spring resort east of Xi'an where Chiang Kai-shek was lodged; his flight up the hillside in his nightclothes when Zhang's troops came for him at dawn on 12 December became one of the famous images of the incident.

ch03.anchor: Song Qiyun, Yang Hucheng's secretary
ch03.note: Song Qiyun (1904-1949), a secret Communist who served as Yang Hucheng's secretary and ran the Northwest Culture Daily as a cover; arrested with his family in 1941, he was killed by Kuomintang agents in 1949. His small son, murdered with him, is remembered in China as 'the little turnip head.' (The source prints his surname as 宗 Zong here at first mention and as 宋 Song at his fuller introduction and in the photograph caption; Song is the attested form, adopted throughout.)

ch03.anchor: at Laoshan and Yulinqiao
ch03.note: Two Red Army victories over the Northeastern Army in northern Shaanxi in the autumn of 1935: at Laoshan (1 October) a division was destroyed, and at Yulinqiao later that month the 619th Regiment. The heavy losses helped turn Zhang Xueliang toward a truce.

ch03.anchor: captured its commander, Gao Fuyuan
ch03.note: Gao Fuyuan (1901-1937), the captured regimental commander who, won over in captivity, became the first secret go-between carrying letters between the Red Army and Zhang Xueliang. He was shot in 1937 by hardline Northeastern Army officers in the turmoil that followed the incident.

ch03.anchor: Wang Yizhe's 107th Division
ch03.note: Wang Yizhe (1896-1937), a senior Northeastern Army commander and confidant of Zhang Xueliang who took part in the secret dealings with the Communists. He was assassinated on 2 February 1937 by young hardline officers of his own army in the factional bloodletting after the Xi'an Incident.

ch03.anchor: then Peng Dehuai came to talk with him
ch03.note: Peng Dehuai (1898-1974), one of the Red Army's foremost commanders, later a marshal of the People's Republic and its defense minister until Mao purged him in 1959; he died in disgrace during the Cultural Revolution.

ch03.anchor: Wang Feng was sent to make contact
ch03.note: Wang Feng (1910-1998), a Shaanxi Communist who carried Mao's personal letter to Yang Hucheng and opened the Party's direct contact with him; he later held senior posts in the People's Republic, including work on ethnic affairs and as a provincial leader.

ch03.anchor: with Wang Shiying, Nan Hanchen, Chen Yangshan
ch03.note: Wang Shiying (1905-1968), a veteran Communist intelligence officer under the Military Commission, active in the united-front work with the northwestern generals; he died under persecution in the Cultural Revolution. Nan Hanchen (1895-1967), Yang Hucheng's former chief secretary, became the first governor of the People's Bank of China in the new state.

ch03.anchor: Yang's 38th Army (commanded by Zhao Shoushan)
ch03.note: Zhao Shoushan (1894-1965), a general of Yang Hucheng's who quietly sheltered a Party underground in his ranks and openly went over to the Communists in 1949, afterward serving as a provincial governor.

ch03.anchor: the New 35th Division (commanded by Kong Congzhou)
ch03.note: Kong Congzhou (1906-1991), a secret Communist within Yang Hucheng's forces who later became a general of the People's Liberation Army.

ch03.anchor: go and look up Mr. Du Binchen
ch03.note: Du Binchen (1888-1947), a Shaanxi educator and statesman close to Yang Hucheng and sympathetic to the Communists; he was executed by the Kuomintang in 1947.

ch03.anchor: August First Declaration
ch03.note: The 'August First Declaration' of 1 August 1935, issued from Moscow in the name of the Chinese Communist Party and the Chinese Soviet government, called on all parties and armies to stop the civil war and unite against Japan; it was an early public statement of the united-front line.

ch03.anchor: had sent Shen Bochun to see him there
ch03.note: Shen Bochun (1898-1979), a go-between in the early contacts with Yang Hucheng, later an official in the People's Republic.

ch03.anchor: one of his division commanders, Feng Qinzai
ch03.note: Feng Qinzai (1889-1963), a division commander under Yang Hucheng who broke with him and sided with Chiang at the time of the Xi'an Incident.

ch03.anchor: the Communist Yan Kuiyao
ch03.note: Yan Kuiyao (1904-1994), then a regimental commander in Yang Hucheng's forces and a secret Communist, later a lieutenant general and senior staff officer of the People's Liberation Army.

ch03.anchor: help Wu Xiru run the Cultural Weekly
ch03.note: Wu Xiru (1906-1985), a left-wing writer and Communist who edited the Cultural Weekly under the cover of Zhang Xueliang's Northeastern Army.

ch03.anchor: the left-wing writers Xu Pingyu and Ding Ling
ch03.note: Ding Ling (1904-1986), one of the best-known writers of the Chinese left, whose fiction of women's lives had made her famous before she reached the Communist areas; she would herself fall foul of the very campaigns this chapter describes. Xu Pingyu (1909-1986) was a left-wing writer and, in the People's Republic, a cultural official.

ch03.anchor: founded by the Anti-Japanese Comrades' Association
ch03.note: The Anti-Japanese Comrades' Association (Kang-Ri Tongzhi Hui), a secret patriotic body within Zhang Xueliang's Northeastern Army that pressed for resistance to Japan and cooperation with the Communists.

ch03.anchor: Red China News Agency
ch03.note: The Red China News Agency (Hongse Zhonghua Tongxunshe), the Communist Party's wire service in the Soviet areas and the direct forerunner of the New China (Xinhua) News Agency; its Xi'an branch relayed Party news and documents during the united-front period.

ch03.anchor: Li Yimang of the Shaanxi provincial committee
ch03.note: Li Yimang (1903-1990), a writer and Party official, later prominent in the People's Republic's cultural and foreign-liaison work.

ch03.anchor: the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region
ch03.note: The Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, the Communist base around Yan'an spanning parts of Shaanxi, Gansu, and Ningxia, and the Party's seat of government through the war years.

ch03.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek's loyal general Hu Zongnan
ch03.note: Hu Zongnan (1896-1962), the Whampoa-trained general Chiang trusted to hold the northwest and blockade the Communist base at Yan'an; his headquarters made Xi'an a nerve center of Nationalist intelligence.

ch03.anchor: with Wu Defeng in charge
ch03.note: Wu Defeng (1896-1976), head of the Party's Xi'an intelligence station, later a mayor of Wuhan and a judicial official in the People's Republic.

ch03.anchor: the Lugou Bridge Incident of July 1937
ch03.note: The Lugou Bridge, or Marco Polo Bridge, Incident of 7 July 1937, the clash outside Beijing that opened the full-scale war between China and Japan.

ch03.anchor: Chen worked with Nan Hanchen, Liu Ding, Xuan Xiafu, Xu Binru
ch03.note: Xuan Xiafu (1899-1938), a Communist active in united-front and military work, murdered by Kuomintang agents in 1938; Xu Binru (1901-1980), a Communist historian later prominent in the museums of the People's Republic.

ch03.anchor: such as Du Binchen, Li Furen, Gao Chongmin, Yang Mingxuan
ch03.note: Prominent Xi'an patriots of the resistance period: Li Furen (1895-1975), a journalist and educator; Gao Chongmin (1891-1971), a founder of the China Democratic League; Yang Mingxuan (1891-1967), an educator and later a vice-governor of Shaanxi; with them Han Zhuoru, Che Xiangchen, and Xu Zhongquan, figures of the local resistance and cultural world.

ch03.anchor: the Central Social Affairs Department at Yan'an
ch03.note: The Central Social Affairs Department (Zhongyang Shehui Bu), the Party's central intelligence and security organ, set up in 1939 under Kang Sheng; it directed both foreign intelligence and internal security and was an ancestor of the later state security services.

ch03.anchor: sponsored by Comrades Luo Qingchang and Qiu Jin
ch03.note: Luo Qingchang (1918-2014), a career intelligence officer who rose to head the Party's investigation department in later decades. The Qiu Jin here is a Yan'an cadre, not the revolutionary martyr of 1907 whose name has the same sound.

ch03.anchor: Elder Sister Deng Yingchao
ch03.note: Deng Yingchao (1904-1992), a women's leader and Zhou Enlai's wife, herself a veteran revolutionary; 'Elder Sister Deng' (Deng dajie) was the affectionate name comrades used for her.

ch03.anchor: just then Yan'an was launching the Rectification Movement
ch03.note: The Yan'an Rectification Movement (zhengfeng, 1942-1945), the Party's campaign to unify thought around Mao's line through study, criticism, and self-criticism. It consolidated Mao's leadership; but its later cadre-vetting phase, driven by Kang Sheng, turned into the persecutions this chapter goes on to describe.

ch03.anchor: study at the Central Party School
ch03.note: The Central Party School at Yan'an, the Party's senior training academy; Mao took over as its principal in 1943, making it a center of the Rectification.

ch03.anchor: Wu Xiru and Wang Shiwei
ch03.note: Wang Shiwei (1906-1947), a writer at Yan'an whose essay 'Wild Lilies' attacked privilege and inequality among the leadership; made a central target of the Rectification, branded a Trotskyite, and secretly executed in 1947. His case became a byword for the campaign's excesses, and he was posthumously cleared in 1991. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: It was in these three branches that Jiang Qing and Ye Qun were vetted
ch03.note: Jiang Qing (1914-1991), a former Shanghai actress who married Mao Zedong in Yan'an and, three decades later, led the ultra-left Gang of Four in the Cultural Revolution, to be tried and imprisoned after Mao's death. Ye Qun (1917-1971), who married the marshal Lin Biao, died with him in the 1971 plane crash after his failed move against Mao. That the young Chen Yangshan's branch reviewed the wartime histories of both women is among the striking details of this account.

ch03.anchor: the "Three People's Principles Youth Corps"
ch03.note: The Three People's Principles Youth Corps (Sanqingtuan), the Kuomintang's youth organization, founded in 1938; membership in it was treated in the Rectification as the mark of a suspect past.

ch03.anchor: the so-called "Movement to Rescue the Fallen" was launched
ch03.note: The 'Movement to Rescue the Fallen' (qiangjiu shizuzhe) of 1943, the coercive high point of the Rectification's cadre-vetting, in which Kang Sheng's methods extracted mass false confessions of spying; thousands were wrongly branded enemy agents before Mao ordered the campaign reined in. Later Party verdicts admit these excesses. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: The Party's Seventh Congress was also about to open
ch03.note: The Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party in fact met from 23 April to 11 June 1945, not 1943 as this and the following paragraphs have it. The error is the source's; Mao's own words below, on 'the twenty-four years of our Party's course,' count from the Party's founding in 1921 to 1945, and the membership figures given (1.2 million members, nearly a million troops) are those of 1945. The congress enshrined Mao Zedong Thought in the Party constitution and chose the leadership that would win the civil war.

ch03.anchor: with Mao Zedong himself as principal and Peng Zhen as deputy
ch03.note: Peng Zhen (1902-1997), a leading Party organizer, later mayor of Beijing and the first senior figure purged at the outset of the Cultural Revolution; rehabilitated, he helped rebuild the legal system in the 1980s.

ch03.anchor: Ren Bishi first reported on how the congress had been prepared
ch03.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950), one of the five secretaries of the Party's wartime leadership alongside Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, and Zhu De; he died young, in 1950.

ch03.anchor: The "Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of the Party,"
ch03.note: The 'Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of the Party,' adopted in 1945, was the Party's authoritative reckoning with its past line struggles; it fixed the verdict that Mao's leadership had rescued the revolution from a succession of erroneous lines.

ch03.anchor: Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, Lin Boqu, and Okano Susumu
ch03.note: Zhu De (1886-1976), commander-in-chief of the Red Army and later the People's Liberation Army; Liu Shaoqi (1898-1969), the Party's leading organizer and later head of state, who died in prison during the Cultural Revolution; Lin Boqu (1886-1960), a revolutionary elder. Okano Susumu was the alias used in Yan'an by Nosaka Sanzo (1892-1993), a founder of the Japanese Communist Party who spent the war years with the Chinese Communists organizing anti-war work among Japanese prisoners.

ch03.anchor: "On Coalition Government," and had a copy given to every delegate
ch03.note: 'On Coalition Government,' Mao Zedong's political report to the Seventh Congress in 1945, set out the Communist program for the end of the war and after: a coalition to replace one-party Kuomintang rule, and the building of a 'new-democratic' China.

ch03.anchor: again proposed five Marxist-Leninist works
ch03.note: The five works were the touchstones of orthodox Marxism-Leninism then: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto and Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific; Lenin's Two Tactics of Social-Democracy in the Democratic Revolution and 'Left-Wing' Communism, an Infantile Disorder; and the Stalin-era History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks), the 'Short Course.'

ch03.anchor: studying at Zaoyuan in Yan'an
ch03.note: Zaoyuan, 'the orchard,' a compound outside Yan'an that housed the Party's central leadership and the Social Affairs Department in the war years.

ch03.anchor: the "April Third Decision,"
ch03.note: The 'April Third Decision' properly names the Central Committee's decision of 3 April 1943 on carrying the Rectification forward; this recollection places it in the spring of 1942, when the Rectification was first launched.

ch03.anchor: the Investigation Bureau of the Jin-Sui Military Region
ch03.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Military Region, a Communist command in northwestern Shanxi and beyond under He Long; its investigation bureau handled intelligence and security.

ch03.anchor: Kirov, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPSU Central Committee
ch03.note: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad Party boss, was assassinated on 1 December 1934; Stalin used his murder as the pretext for the purges and show trials that became the Great Terror of 1936-1938. The 'third year' places this account in 1937, at the Terror's height.

ch03.anchor: The head of the CCP delegation to the Communist International was Wang Ming
ch03.note: The Communist International, or Comintern, was the Moscow-based body directing the world's Communist parties. Wang Ming (Chen Shaoyu, 1904-1974) led the 'returned students' faction and the CCP delegation to the Comintern; his rivalry with Mao runs through the Party's history of these years, and he spent his last decades in the Soviet Union attacking Mao.

ch03.anchor: suppress counter-revolutionaries and root out Trotskyites
ch03.note: The Soviet purge and its anti-Trotskyist drive swept up foreign Communists resident in the USSR along with Soviet citizens; a number of Chinese Communists studying or working in Moscow were arrested and shot in 1937-1938. That these deaths happened is well attested; how far Kang Sheng personally engineered particular cases, as the book charges, rests largely on testimony gathered in China after his fall.

ch03.anchor: several of the chief men Kang Sheng named: Xiao Shouhuang, Ouyang Xin, He Changzhi
ch03.note: Xiao Shouhuang, Ouyang Xin, and He Changzhi were Chinese Communist cadres, formerly of the Central Special Branch, sent to study in the Soviet Union in 1935 and killed there in the purge of 1937-1938. The Party rehabilitated them after 1978. The book gives their names as Chen Yangshan remembered them; some appear in other records under variant characters.

ch03.anchor: Wu Hujing was a Shandong man
ch03.note: Wu Hujing (1904-1938), also known as Wu Huairang, a senior Communist organizer who had led the Party's work in northern Manchuria and in the Central Special Branch; sent to Moscow in 1935, he was arrested and shot in the Soviet purge. His wife was the revolutionary Hou Zhi. He was posthumously rehabilitated.

ch03.anchor: Kang Sheng's own sister-in-law, Su Mei
ch03.note: Su Mei was a sister of Kang Sheng's wife, Cao Yi'ou; that she went to the Soviet Union with the others yet came to no harm is the circumstantial point Chen Yangshan presses against Kang.

ch03.anchor: Kang Sheng was head of its Action Section
ch03.note: The Action Section (xingdong ke) was the Special Branch's armed arm, the 'Red Squad' whose killings of traitors filled the previous chapter; Kang Sheng directed it in the early 1930s.

ch03.anchor: the anti-Party crimes of Lin Biao and the "Gang of Four"
ch03.note: Lin Biao (1907-1971), the marshal named as Mao's successor, who died in a plane crash over Mongolia in 1971 after an alleged plot against Mao. The Gang of Four (Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen) were the ultra-left leaders of the Cultural Revolution, arrested in 1976; the reckoning with their 'crimes' was the moment Chen Yangshan's charges against Kang Sheng were laid before the Party.

ch03.anchor: there must be no "coercion, confession, and credence."
ch03.note: 'Coercion, confession, credence' (bi, gong, xin): the vicious circle in which torture ('coercion') produces false confessions, which are then 'believed' and used to force fresh arrests. Mao's warnings against it, quoted here, were aimed at the very campaign Kang Sheng was running.

ch03.anchor: in the days of the Central Soviet Area
ch03.note: The Central Soviet Area in Jiangxi (1931-1934), the Communists' main base before the Long March, where an earlier internal purge (the anti-'AB' campaign, and the Futian Incident of 1930) had killed many of the Party's own; that was the bitter lesson Mao invokes.

ch03.anchor: in 1980 the Party Center decided to expel him from the Party
ch03.note: Kang Sheng (1898-1975) died honored; only in 1980, as the Party reckoned with the Cultural Revolution, was he posthumously expelled and his ashes removed from the Babaoshan cemetery of revolutionary martyrs. It is this official verdict that lets the book state his guilt so flatly.

ch03.anchor: To the Central Organization Department, and to the Ministry of State Security
ch03.note: The Ministry of State Security, the People's Republic's civilian intelligence and security ministry, was formed in 1983; its inclusion as an addressee fits the letter's 1988 date.

ch03.anchor: Xiao Shouhuang (from Dapu, Guangdong)
ch03.note: Dapu is the county of Dabu in eastern Guangdong (the source writes the place-name with a homophone). 'Lao Da,' 'Lao Wang,' and 'Lao Hu' that follow are the men's familiar nicknames, not surnames.

ch04.anchor: The Jin-Sui Border Region was one of the principal revolutionary base areas
ch04.note: The Jin-Sui (Shanxi-Suiyuan) Border Region was a Communist base area straddling northwestern Shanxi and the neighboring province of Suiyuan (now largely central Inner Mongolia), established during the war against Japan and led from Xingxian. Its value, as the text says, lay in its position screening the Party's Yan'an headquarters in the Shaan-Gan-Ning region and linking it to the areas beyond; the claim that it was the “one artery” to Outer Mongolia and the Soviet Union is the book's own emphasis, corroborated in broad outline by histories of the base area, which stress its role as a corridor and shield rather than a major fighting front.

ch04.anchor: Luo Qingchang has recalled
ch04.note: Luo Qingchang (1918–2004) was a career Communist intelligence officer who rose to head the Central Investigation Department (the CCP's foreign-intelligence organ) and was long one of Zhou Enlai's trusted men on the hidden front; he is remembered for the deathbed charge Zhou gave him in 1975 concerning Taiwan. At its first appearance here (printed p. 106) the source prints his name with the characters transposed, as “Luo Changqing” (罗长青); it gives the correct form “Luo Qingchang” (罗青长) five pages on. Both are rendered here by the correct name.

ch04.anchor: had Stalingrad fallen, the world revolution would have entered a dark time
ch04.note: The Battle of Stalingrad (August 1942 to February 1943) was the turning point of the Soviet-German war; a German victory there was widely feared at the time to open the way to a Japanese-German linkup across Eurasia. Luo Qingchang's remark reflects the anxiety in Yan'an that the fall of the Soviet Union would have isolated the Chinese revolution.

ch04.anchor: we built a base in the Daqing Mountains
ch04.note: The Daqingshan (Great Blue Mountains) guerrilla base was a Communist foothold in the mountains north of Guisui (Hohhot) in Suiyuan, opened in 1938 by a detachment under Li Jingquan and Yao Zhe; it extended the Jin-Sui area's reach toward Mongolia and the Sino-Soviet frontier.

ch04.anchor: push the "Gao Shuxun Movement" forward vigorously
ch04.note: The “Gao Shuxun Movement” was a Communist campaign, named for the Nationalist general Gao Shuxun, to induce Nationalist officers to defect rather than fight in the civil war.
