Gao (1898–1972), a deputy commander in the Eleventh War Zone, crossed over with his troops at the Handan front on 30 October 1945; Mao Zedong seized on the example and called in early 1946 for the systematic organizing of such revolts. The campaign is treated at length later in this chapter.

ch04.anchor: He Long and Li Jingquan spoke at a public-security conference
ch04.note: Li Jingquan (1909–1989) was a senior political commissar of the Jin-Sui base area and its military region, later first Party secretary of Sichuan and a Politburo member; he was purged in the Cultural Revolution and rehabilitated afterward. He Long, the region's commander and Chen Yangshan's old protector, is introduced earlier in the book.

ch04.anchor: a section of the Bureau of Confidential Investigation's organization in southern Shanxi
ch04.note: The Bureau of Confidential Investigation (Baomiju, 保密局) was the Nationalist secret service formed in 1946 from the wartime Juntong (Bureau of Investigation and Statistics); it ran counter-Communist agent networks until 1949. It recurs through this chapter as the chief adversary of Chen Yangshan's stations.

ch04.anchor: and by Chiang (Kai-shek), Yan (Xishan), and Fu (Zuoyi)
ch04.note: Yan Xishan (1883–1960) was the warlord who governed Shanxi from 1911 until 1949, notorious for keeping thousands of surrendered Japanese troops in his service after 1945 (mentioned below); he fled to Taiwan and briefly served as the Republic of China's premier. Fu Zuoyi (1895–1974) was the Nationalist commander in Suiyuan and later North China, who surrendered Beiping peacefully in January 1949 and went on to serve the People's Republic as minister of water resources. Chiang Kai-shek is noted earlier.

ch04.anchor: secret talks between the puppet forces and Yan Xishan's representatives
ch04.note: After Japan's surrender Yan Xishan raced to take over the puppet garrisons and Japanese arms in Shanxi before the Communists could, and secretly retained several thousand Japanese soldiers (see below) to hold Taiyuan. Communist intelligence tracking these contacts is the subject of much of this chapter.

ch04.anchor: Tan Zhengwen as director and Chen Yangshan as deputy director
ch04.note: Tan Zhengwen (1910–1961) was a leading Communist security official, head of the Jin-Sui public-security apparatus and later a deputy procurator-general of the People's Republic. His transfer in 1947 (noted below) left Chen Yangshan as director.

ch04.anchor: with Ma Mingfang, deputy secretary of the Northwest Bureau
ch04.note: Ma Mingfang (1905–1974) was a veteran Communist organizer of the Shaanxi base areas, later a deputy secretary of the CCP Northwest Bureau and a national labor and organization official; he was persecuted to death in the Cultural Revolution.

ch04.anchor: and it was through the Special Branch, through Comrade Chen Yangshan's arrangements, to be exact, that I was hidden in Shanghai and then secretly moved on to Honghu
ch04.note: Honghu (“Vast Lake”), on the Hubei-Hunan border, was the heart of the Xiang-E-Xi soviet that He Long and Zhou Yiqun built after the Nanchang Uprising of 1927. He Long's escape from Shanghai to Honghu, arranged by the Special Branch, is told in Chapter 1; his gratitude is why he asked for Chen Yangshan by name in 1944.

ch04.anchor: Pei Zhouyu, then deputy director of the Jin-Sui Border Region Public Security Bureau, has recalled
ch04.note: The source appends a biographical note to Pei Zhouyu (裹周玉), translated here: born December 1912, a native of Pingjiang, Hunan; joined the Boy Scouts in 1926 and the Communist Youth League in 1927, took part that year in the local Autumn Harvest Uprising, joined the Red Third Army Group in 1930 and the Party in 1931. He served as squad and platoon leader, divisional youth officer, inspection-section chief of the Third Army Group's security bureau, and divisional special commissioner, and took part in all four counter-encirclement campaigns of the Central Soviet and in the Long March. In the war against Japan he was security-section chief of the 358th Brigade and then of the 120th Division's political department, security head, and deputy chief of the Jin-Sui Public Security Bureau; in the civil war, director of the Suimeng Public Security Bureau and a political-department director in the First Field Army's Eighth Column. After 1949 he held senior political posts in the Volunteer Army in Korea, the 69th Army, the Beijing and Xinjiang military regions, and the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps; made a major general in 1955, he died in Beijing on 12 June 2015, aged 103.

ch04.anchor: Lieutenant General Zhao Jin'ao, to work for us
ch04.note: Zhao Jin'ao is named here as the Nationalist Yanbei (northern Shanxi) security commander whom Pei Zhouyu's network won over in 1938. The claim is the book's; independent corroboration of the name and the episode is thin, and the reading of the uncommon character 鹰 is taken from the scan.

ch04.anchor: the Japanese agents' "Kawasaki Mansion."
ch04.note: The “Kawasaki Mansion” (Chuanqi gongguan) was evidently a cover name for a Japanese special-service (tokumu) station in the Datong area; such fronts, named for their nominal proprietors, were standard Japanese intelligence practice in occupied China.

ch04.anchor: the Japanese Communist friend Okano Susumu
ch04.note: Okano Susumu was the alias under which Nosaka Sanzo (1892–1993), a founder and later chairman of the Japanese Communist Party, spent the war years in Yan'an running anti-war work among Japanese prisoners. He is introduced in Chapter 3. The source here misprints his Japanese name as 野板参三 for 野坊参三 (Nosaka).

ch04.anchor: the Department's Book-and-Press Newsletter agency
ch04.note: The Book-and-Press Newsletter (Shubao Jianxun) was the Central Intelligence Department's digest of the enemy and foreign press, compiled from the material the stations collected and circulated to the Party leadership as open-source intelligence on the enemy situation.

ch04.anchor: On April 13, 1947, Chen Yangshan gave a talk on intelligence work at the joint conference of Jin-Sui public-security chiefs. He said: "After Japan's surrender
ch04.note: This speech, dated 13 April 1947, repeats almost word for word the self-criticism the book places at a joint conference on 13 April 1948 (printed pp. 109–110). The two datings cannot both be right; the source reproduces the passage twice, under different years, without noting the discrepancy, and both are rendered here as printed.

ch04.anchor: our demolition hero Liang Shengyuan
ch04.note: Liang Shengyuan is celebrated here as the saboteur who destroyed the Taiyuan Number Two Powder Works in July 1947. The exploit is recounted a second time later in the chapter; the figures for the munitions destroyed are the book's.

ch04.anchor: into the Association for the Promotion of Democracy to carry on agent work
ch04.note: The China Association for Promoting Democracy (Zhongguo Minzhu Cujinhui), founded in Shanghai in 1945, was one of the “democratic parties” sympathetic to the Communists; the passage describes Nationalist agents trying to penetrate it, and Communist counter-intelligence exposing them.

ch04.anchor: the Twelfth Brigade commander E Yousan
ch04.note: E Yousan (1905–1951) was a Nationalist cavalry commander in Suiyuan under Fu Zuoyi, notorious for his raids into Communist territory; he refused to join Dong Qiwu's peaceful uprising in 1949, fled, and was later captured and executed.

ch04.anchor: Ma Hongkui had sent representatives to secret talks with Dong Qiwu
ch04.note: Ma Hongkui (1892–1970) was the Muslim warlord who ruled Ningxia, one of the “Ma clique” of the northwest; he pressed Dong Qiwu to keep fighting the Communists and fled to Taiwan and then the United States in 1949. Dong Qiwu (1899–1989), Fu Zuoyi's subordinate commanding in Suiyuan, instead led the peaceful “Suiyuan-way” uprising of September 1949 and served the People's Republic afterward; the intelligence his trusted men passed to Chen Yangshan's stations is described near the end of this chapter.

ch04.anchor: the Nationalist takeover officials in Beiping and Tianjin
ch04.note: The source prints “Ping-Lu” (平律) here, evidently a misprint for “Ping-Jin” (平津), the standard abbreviation for Beiping and Tianjin; the surrounding text names both cities, and the sense is followed here. The “fly-in faction” and “underground faction” were the rival cliques of returning and locally planted Nationalist officials who scrambled for the spoils of the takeover.

ch04.anchor: "Say not that the scholar only argues in the void; where the head is flung down, the blood lies in bright stains."
ch04.note: A patriotic couplet in the classical manner, honoring a scholar who dies for his cause rather than merely talking. The source opens it with 没谓 for the usual 莫谓 (“say not”); the lines circulated in the resistance period and are quoted here as the martyr Wang Shukai's epitaph.

ch04.anchor: Gao Shuxun, deputy commander-in-chief of the Nationalist Eleventh War Zone
ch04.note: Gao Shuxun's crossing-over with an army and a column at the Handan (Pinghan railway) front on 30 October 1945 was the first major Nationalist defection of the civil war and gave its name to the campaign described above. He had long been at odds with Chiang Kai-shek's central-army commanders; after 1949 he held military and civil posts under the People's Republic.

ch04.anchor: Pan Shuoduan, commander of the Nationalist 184th Division
ch04.note: Pan Shuoduan (1901–1978) led the 184th Division in revolt at Haicheng in Liaoning on 30 May 1946, the first such uprising in the Northeast; he served the People's Republic afterward as a water-conservancy and provincial official.

ch04.anchor: Captain Liu Shanben of the Nationalist air force's Eighth Flying Squadron
ch04.note: Liu Shanben (1915–1968) flew a B-24 bomber from Chengdu to Yan'an on 26 June 1946, the first Nationalist air-force pilot to defect; he became an instructor in the new People's Liberation Army air force and died during the Cultural Revolution.

ch04.anchor: a regimental commander surnamed Wei of the 320th Division of the enemy Suimeng forces led more than 1,400 men in revolt; in the spring of 1949 a battalion commander surnamed Li
ch04.note: The source withholds the given names of these two defecting Nationalist officers, printing only the surnames Wei (魔) and Li (李) followed by crosses. The redaction is the source's and is kept here.

ch04.anchor: "Let the courage be great and the heart small, the wits round and the conduct square."
ch04.note: A maxim from the Tang physician Sun Simiao (581–682), often quoted as a rule of character: be bold in daring but careful in mind, supple in wits but upright in action. The author applies it to Chen Yangshan's cast of mind.

ch04.anchor: revolutionary principle of "a needle hidden in cotton."
ch04.note: “A needle hidden in cotton” (mian li cang zhen) is a set phrase for a soft exterior over a hard, unyielding core; here it praises the tender wording but firm principle of Chen Yangshan's refusal, in the letter, to bend the marriage rule for a subordinate.

ch04.anchor: the army-organization group of the Work Committee of Yan Xishan's "Comradeship Association."
ch04.note: The Comradeship Association (Tongzhihui), fully the “Comradeship Association for the Sacrifice to Save the Nation,” was Yan Xishan's mass political organization and the instrument of his personal rule in Shanxi; its Work Committee was the inner control body. Wei Jian's rise inside it is what gave the Communist station its reach into Yan's army.

ch04.anchor: ran a "summer progressive discussion session" at Kenanpo
ch04.note: Kenanpo (“Slope of Surmounted Hardship”), in Ji County on the Yellow River in southwestern Shanxi, was Yan Xishan's wartime seat of government from 1940 after the Japanese took Taiyuan; the fortified hill complex described here ringed it.

ch04.anchor: Yan Xishan's fifth sister Yan Huiqing
ch04.note: Yan Huiqing, known as the “Fifth Miss,” was a kinswoman and confidante of Yan Xishan who managed much of his household and secretariat; she died with his regime at the fall of Taiyuan in April 1949. The book's account of her papers being rifled is the kind of hidden-front episode it favors and rests on the participants' recollections.

ch04.anchor: the Jiefang Daily printed the document in full
ch04.note: The Jiefang Daily (Liberation Daily) was the Communist Party's chief newspaper, published in Yan'an from 1941; printing the captured minutes in full was a propaganda blow against the staged Nationalist press tour.

ch04.anchor: Zhou Enlai, Marshall, and Zhang Zhizhong formed a three-man mediation group
ch04.note: The “Committee of Three” of early 1946 paired the Communist Zhou Enlai and the Nationalist Zhang Zhizhong (1890–1969), a general known for his conciliatory line who later crossed to the Communist side, with the American envoy George C. Marshall, sent by President Truman to broker a truce. The mediation collapsed into full civil war within the year.

ch04.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek's chief of the general staff Chen Cheng
ch04.note: Chen Cheng (1898–1965) was one of Chiang Kai-shek's most trusted commanders, chief of the general staff during the civil war and later premier and vice-president of the Republic of China on Taiwan; his visit to Taiyuan to whip up the war effort is the scene sketched here.

ch04.anchor: try to win a puppet National Assembly seat
ch04.note: The National Assembly (Guomin Dahui) that the Nationalists convened in November 1946, boycotted by the Communists, was denounced by them as a rubber-stamp body; hence “puppet.” A seat in it would have given the Communist agent Wu Zhezhi legal cover and access.

ch04.anchor: Wu brought 400,000 puppet fabi back from Yan'an
ch04.note: Fabi (“legal tender”) was the Nationalist paper currency; by 1945 runaway inflation had gutted its value, so a sum like 400,000 was modest working capital. The book calls it “puppet” fabi as enemy money.

ch04.anchor: copied it into an account book with a writing brush dipped in milk
ch04.note: Milk was a common improvised invisible ink: written with a brush it dries clear and shows up brown when the paper is later heated. Copying the reorganization plan this way let the agent hide it in plain sight in an ordinary ledger.

ch04.anchor: vetting work left over from the "Rescue Movement,"
ch04.note: The “Rescue Movement” (Qiangjiu yundong) of 1943 was the coercive, confession-driven phase of the Yan'an Rectification, in which many cadres were wrongly branded spies; Mao Zedong later ordered the excesses corrected. The “vetting” (zhenbie) Chen Yangshan is sent to finish was the case-by-case clearing of those wrongly accused. The movement is treated in Chapter 3.
